paragraphs: She started crying again, but she kept a tight grip on Mitya’s hand and wouldn’t let it go.

“Mitya, dear, stay here, don’t leave. There’s one thing I want to tell you,” she whispered, and all at once looked up into his face. “Listen. Tell me who it is I love. There’s one man here I love. Who is he? You’re the one who has to tell me.”
Her tear-swollen face lit up with a smile, and her eyes glittered in the dim light.

“In flew a falcon, and my heart dropped. ‘Fool, that’s the man you love!’ my heart whispered to me at once. Then you walked in and everything lit up. What’s he scared of? I wondered. You were frightened, you couldn’t say a word. It’s not those people he’s afraid of—could he be scared of anyone? It’s me he’s afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you silly, that I called out of the window to Alyosha that I’d loved Mityenka for one hour, and that now I was off to love ... somebody else. Mitya, Mitya, what a fool I was, to think I could love anybody after you! Will you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or don’t you? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She leaped up and took him by the shoulders with both hands. Mitya, struck dumb with rapture, looked into her eyes, her face, her smile, and then suddenly crushed her in his arms and kissed her passionately.

“Forgive me for making you suffer, won’t you? I made you all suffer out of spite. Out of spite I drove the old man out of his mind.... Remember the day you were drinking at my place and smashed the wine glass? I remembered that, and today I smashed a glass too and drank ‘to my vile heart.’ Mitya, my falcon, why won’t you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he draws back, looking and listening. Why are you listening to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, yes, like that. If you love, then love! I’ll be your slave now, your slave all my life. Slavery is sweet. Kiss me! Beat me, treat me badly, do what you want with me.... I deserve to suffer, I do. Wait, stop, later, I won’t have it....” and she shoved him away all at once. “Off with you, Mitya, I’ll come and have some wine, I want to be drunk, I’ll get drunk and dance; I have to, I have to!” She wrenched herself free and vanished behind the curtain. Mitya went after her like a drunken man.

“Yes, come what may, whatever happens now, for a single minute I’d give the whole world,” he thought. Grushenka really did gulp down a full glass of champagne in one swallow, and was at once very tipsy. She sat in the same chair as before, smiling blissfully. Her cheeks were aglow, her lips were burning, her shining eyes were wet; they were full of passionate appeal. Even Kalganov felt his heart stir, and he went over to her.

“Did you feel it, when I kissed you while you were asleep just now?” she said in a thick voice. “I’m drunk, that’s all it is.... And you, aren’t you drunk? And why isn’t Mitya drinking? Mitya, why don’t you drink? I’m drunk and you’re not drinking....”
“I’m drunk! I’m drunk anyway ... drunk on you ... and now I’ll get drunk on wine too.”

He emptied another glass, and—he found it strange himself—that one glass made him completely drunk. All at once he was drunk, though up to then he had been quite sober; he remembered that. From that moment the world spun around him, as in a fever. He walked about, laughed, talked to everyone, not knowing what he did. Only one burning sensation stayed with him all the time, “like a red-hot coal in his heart,” as he said later. He went to her, sat down next to her, looked at her, listened to her.... She grew very talkative and kept calling everyone over, beckoning to one girl after another from the chorus. When a girl came up, Grushenka would kiss her or make the sign of the cross over her. Another minute and she might have cried. The “little old man,” as she called Maximov, amused her enormously. He kept running up to kiss her hands, “every little finger,” and at last he danced another dance, to an old song he sang himself. He put special vigor into the refrain:

The little pig says—umph! umph! umph! The little calf says—moo, moo, moo, The little duck says—quack, quack, quack, The little goose says—ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say!

“Give him something, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Give him a present, he’s poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted!... You know what, Mitya, I’m going to enter a nunnery. I will, I mean it, someday. Alyosha told me something today that I’ll remember as long as I live.... Yes.... But today we dance. Nunnery tomorrow, dancing today. I want to have my fun today, good people, so what? God will forgive us. If I were God, I’d forgive everybody: ‘My dear sinners, from this day on you’re forgiven.’ And I’ll go and ask forgiveness myself: ‘Forgive me, good people, I’m a silly wench.’ I’m a beast, that’s what I am. But I want to pray. I gave away a little onion. Wicked as I’ve been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don’t stop them. Everybody in the world is good. Everybody—even the worst. It’s a nice world. We may be bad, but the world’s all right. We’re good and bad, good and bad.... Come on, tell me, there’s something I want to ask you: come here, all of you, and I’ll ask you: Why am I so good? You know I’m good. I’m very good.... Come on, why am I so good?”

Grushenka went on babbling like this, getting drunker and drunker. At last she declared that she would dance too. She rose from her chair, swaying. “Mitya, give me no more wine—even if I ask, don’t give it to me. Wine brings no peace. Everything’s spinning, the stove and everything. I want to dance. Let everybody see how I dance ... let them see how beautifully I dance....”

She meant it. She took a white cambric handkerchief from her pocket and held it by one corner in her right hand, ready to wave it in the dance. Mitya dashed about, the girls went quiet, ready to burst into a dancing song at the first signal. When Maximov heard that Grushenka wanted to dance, he squealed with delight and went skipping about in front of her, humming:
With legs so slim and sides so trim And its little tail curled tight.
But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and chased him away.
“Sh-h! Mitya, why aren’t they coming? Let them all come ... and watch. Call in the ones you locked up, too.... Why did you lock them in? Tell them I’m going to dance. Let them watch too....”
With a drunken swagger Mitya went to the locked door and began pounding on it with his fist, calling the Poles.
“Hey, you ... Podvysotskys! Come out, she’s going to dance. She’s asking for you.”
“_Lajdak!_” one of the Poles shouted in answer.
“You’re a _lajdak_ yourself! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what you are.”
“Stop laughing at Poland,” Kalganov said sententiously. He was drunk as well.
“Hush, boy! If I call him a scoundrel, I haven’t called the whole of Poland that. One _lajdak_ doesn’t make a Poland. Hush, my pretty boy, and eat some candy.”

“Ach, what fellows! As if they weren’t human. Why won’t they be friends?” said Grushenka, and she went forward to dance. The chorus struck up “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka tossed back her head, parted her lips a little, smiled, waved her handkerchief—and suddenly, lurching violently, she stopped in the middle of the room, bewildered.
“I’m weak....” she said, worn out. “Forgive me.... I’m weak, I can’t.... I’m sorry.”
She bowed to the chorus, and then started bowing to everyone, in every direction.
“I’m sorry.... Forgive me....”
“The lady’s been at the drink. The pretty lady’s been drinking,” voices said.
“The lady’s had a drop too much,” Maximov explained to the girls with a giggle.
“Mitya, take me away ... lead me off,” said Grushenka, helpless. Mitya pounced on her, scooped her up in his arms and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

“Well, time for me to go,” thought Kalganov, and he left the blue room, closing both halves of the door behind him. But the orgy in the big room went on, getting louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

“Don’t touch me....” she begged faintly. “Don’t touch me until I’m yours.... I told you I’m yours, but don’t touch me ... spare me.... Not with them here, right next door. He’s here. It’s foul here....”
“I’ll do as you say! I won’t even think of it ... I worship you!” Mitya muttered. “Yes, it’s foul here, it’s disgusting.”
And still holding her, he dropped to his knees by the bed.

“I know you’re a brute, but you’re generous,” Grushenka brought out with difficulty. “It has to be honorable ... from now on it will be honorable ... and let’s be honest, let’s be good, not brutes, but good ... take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don’t want it here, but far, far away....”
“Oh yes, yes, it has to be!” said Mitya, hugging her to him. “I’ll take you and we’ll fly away.... Oh, I’d give my whole life for one year only, to learn about that blood!”
“What blood?” asked Grushenka, confused.
“Nothing,” Mitya muttered between his teeth. “Grusha, you wanted to be honest, and I’m a thief. I’ve stolen money from Katya.... What a disgrace, what a disgrace!”

“From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn’t steal it. Give it back, take it from me.... Why make such a fuss? All I have is yours now. What does money matter? We’ll squander it anyway.... People like us can’t help squandering money. Better that we go and work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We have to work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won’t be your mistress, I’ll be true to you, I’ll be your slave, I’ll work for you. The two of us will go to the young lady and bow down to her, so she’ll forgive us, and then we’ll leave. And if she doesn’t forgive us, we’ll go anyway. Take her the money and love me.... Don’t love her.... Don’t love her anymore. If you love her, I’ll strangle her.... I’ll poke both her eyes out with a needle....”
“I love you. You are the only one I love. I’ll love you in Siberia....”

“Why Siberia? Fine, Siberia, if you want. I don’t care ... we’ll work ... Siberia has snow.... I love riding in the snow ... and there must be bells.... Listen, is that a bell ringing? Where’s that bell coming from? People are coming.... It’s stopped now.”

She shut her eyes, worn out, and dropped off to sleep for a moment. A bell had certainly sounded in the distance, but it had stopped ringing. Mitya let his head fall on her breast. He didn’t notice that the bell had stopped, or that the singing had stopped too, and that in place of songs and drunken uproar there was a dead silence in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

“What is it? Did I sleep? Yes ... a bell ... I was asleep, and I dreamed I was riding over the snow with bells, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved, with you. Far, far away. I was hugging you and kissing you, snuggling up to you. I was cold, and the snow was sparkling.... You know how snow sparkles at night when the moon is out. It was as if I wasn’t on earth. I woke up, and my darling is next to me. How sweet that is!...”

“Next to you,” murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her bosom, her hands. And suddenly a strange notion struck him: she seemed to be staring straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but above his head, with an intent, almost eerie fixity. A look of wonder, almost of alarm, suddenly came over her face.
“Mitya, who is that, watching us?” she whispered.
Mitya turned, and saw that someone had in fact pulled the curtains apart and seemed to be watching them. And it seemed to be more than one person.
He leaped up and strode quickly toward the intruder.
“Here, come over here, to us,” said a voice, not loud, but firm and peremptory.

Mitya went through to the other side of the curtain and froze. The room was full of people, but not the ones who’d been there before. A sudden chill ran down his spine, and he shuddered. He knew every one of them at once. The tall, stout old man in the overcoat and the forage cap with a cockade was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And the “consumptive-looking” dandy, so neat, “who always has such polished boots,” was the deputy prosecutor. “He has a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me.” And the small young man in spectacles.... Mitya had forgotten his surname, though he knew him and had seen him: he was the “investigating lawyer,” from the “school of jurisprudence,” newly arrived in town. And this one was the inspector of police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a man he knew well. And those fellows wearing brass plates, what were they doing here? And those other two ... peasants.... And over there at the door, Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch....
“Gentlemen! What’s the meaning of this, gentlemen?” Mitya began, but all at once, as if he were out of his mind, with no idea what he was doing, he shouted at the top of his voice:
“I un—der—stand!”
The young man in spectacles stepped briskly forward to Mitya and began, with dignity but hurriedly:
“We have to make ... in short, I must ask you to step this way, over to the sofa.... You absolutely must give an explanation.”
“The old man!” Mitya shouted wildly. “The old man and his blood!... I understand.”
And he sank, nearly collapsed, into a chair beside him, as though he had been mown down by a scythe.
“You understand? He understands! Monster, parricide! Your father’s blood cries out against you!” the old police captain bellowed suddenly, coming up to Mitya.
He was out of his mind with rage, red in the face and shaking all over.
“This is impossible!” cried the small young man. “Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won’t do!... Allow me to speak, please. I’d never have expected such conduct from you....”

“This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium,” the police captain cried. “Look at him: drunk, at this hour of the night, with a disreputable woman, his father’s blood on his hands.... It’s delirium!...”
“Dear Mihail Makarovitch, I most earnestly ask you to control yourself,” the prosecutor said in a quick whisper to the old police captain, “or I’ll be forced to resort to—”
But the little lawyer wouldn’t let him finish. He turned to Mitya and said, in a loud, firm, dignified voice:
“Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, I must inform you that you are charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed tonight....”
He said something more, and the prosecutor put in a word as well, but Mitya, though he heard them, did not take it in. He stared at them all with wild eyes.
